facts.statement: The holotype specimen AMNH 3018 is a single tooth about one centimetre long that is elongated, recurved, lacks serrations, has low vertical ridges, and features a D-shaped cross-section with a flattened inner side.
facts.quote: The holotype is specimen AMNH 3018. It is a tooth about one centimetre long, elongated, recurved, lacking serrations, possessing low vertical ridges and with a D-shaped cross-section, the inner side being flattened.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope initially thought the holotype tooth belonged to a plesiosaur but realized within the same year that it represented a carnivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: Cope at first thought the tooth belonged to a plesiosaur, but in the same year realised it represented a carnivorous dinosaur.

facts.statement: The second species Paronychodon caperatus is known from the Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, Montana, and South Dakota, as well as the Lance Formation of Wyoming, dating to the latest Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: A second species, Paronychodon caperatus, is known from the Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, Montana, and South Dakota and Lance Formation of Wyoming (latest Maastrichtian stage, million years ago)

facts.statement: Paronychodon caperatus is based on holotype YPM 10624, a tooth similar in form to P. lacustris but somewhat larger.
facts.quote: It is based on holotype YPM 10624, a tooth close in form to the holotype of P. lacustris but somewhat larger.

facts.statement: In 1995, George Olshevsky renamed Laelaps explanatus to Paronychodon explanatus, though this taxon is now considered to be based on teeth from Saurornitholestes.
facts.quote: In 1995 Olshevsky renamed Laelaps explanatus Cope 1876 into a Paronychodon explanatus; today the taxon is seen as based on Saurornitholestes teeth.

facts.statement: Many specimens referred to Paronychodon include varied teeth such as serrated ones, low ones, and those without a flattened side.
facts.quote: Some of these included serrated teeth, low teeth and teeth without a flattened side.

facts.statement: Paronychodon has been classified variously as a coelurid, ornithomimosaur, dromaeosaurid, archaeopterygid, or troodontid, though it may be another type of coelurosaurian theropod.
facts.quote: Paronychodon has been considered a coelurid, an ornithomimosaur, a dromaeosaurid, an archaeopterygid, and a troodontid, though it could also be another kind of coelurosaurian theropod.

facts.statement: While most researchers consider Paronychodon to represent indeterminate theropod teeth, a small consensus suggests the teeth belong to Deinonychosauria.
facts.quote: While most researchers have therefore considered it simply represents indeterminate theropod teeth, a small consensus has found them to be Deinonychosauria.

facts.statement: No jaws from adult individuals bearing identical Paronychodon teeth have ever been found.
facts.quote: Jaws from adult individuals bearing identical teeth have never been found.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh suggested that Paronychodon teeth were pathological, formed when lower jaw teeth accidentally grew back-to-back on the mandible suture.
facts.quote: Marsh already suggested such teeth were pathological, having formed when the first teeth of the lower jaws by accident grew back-to-back to each other on the mandible suture.

facts.statement: The family classification for Paronychodon is tentatively listed as Troodontidae.
Paronychodon lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, 70 million years ago, during the Maastrichtian in North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, 70 millones de años, en el Maastrichtiense, en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The time range for Paronychodon is recorded from the Kimmeridgian to the Maastrichtian, spanning from 154.8 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Maastrichtian (154.8 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.quote: The type species, named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1876, is Paronychodon lacustris, from the Judith River Formation of Montana, dating to 75 million years ago, during the Campanian stage.

rejected.statement: Teeth of the general Paronychodon type have been reported from various times and places, including the Early Cretaceous Una Formation of Spain dating to 125 million years ago.
rejected.quote: These teeth of the general "Paronychodon" type have been reported from a wide variety of times and places, including the Early Cretaceous Una Formation of Spain, dating to the late Barremian age 125 million years ago.

rejected.quote: Philip J. Currie in 1990 also concluded to a malformation, thinking the flattened side resulted from the tooth remaining attached too long to the inner wall of the tooth-socket.
